title.analysis: Authentic title "Why The Middle Class Is Being Taxed Into Poverty" makes a strong causal claim. The script follows a composite family through a year of taxes, premiums, child care and repairs, then argues the system shifted the tax mix from corporations to payroll. Late in the video it concedes "The middle class isn't being taxed more overall", contradicting the literal title, and most of the squeeze it shows comes from non-tax costs (child care, premiums, repairs). The budget arithmetic also contains a ~$1,000/month error. TYPICAL against the cohort. Association only.

script.opening_words: You're sitting at your kitchen table on a Tuesday night with your laptop open, a calculator app on your phone, and a stack of paper spread out in front of you. Property tax bill, health insurance statement, daycare invoice, student loan payment confirmation. Your spouse is doing dishes in the background, and you're trying to figure out where the hell all the money goes. You make $110,000 combined. Six figures. That used to mean something, right? That used to mean
script.ending_words: corporations went from 28% of federal revenue to 9%. Show them that billionaires pay 3.4% while the Andersons pay 56% when you count everything. The problem isn't them. The problem isn't you. The problem is a machine designed to extract everything it can from people who work for a living while the people who own things pay almost nothing and it's running exactly the way it was built to run.
script.analysis: Full 18980 canonical characters read. Single-narrator composite-family narrative: kitchen-table hook; the Andersons ($110K, two kids); paycheck deductions; property tax; federal return and child tax credit; refund spent; FICA; annual tax-plus-premium total; daycare; monthly budget; invisible taxes; AC, braces, tires, transmission debts; parent's medical bill; then structural argument (corporate vs payroll share of revenue, corporate rates and zero-tax companies, SS wage cap, capital gains, OECD tax-to-GDP, health/child care/tuition comparisons, Germany, wealth concentration, CEO pay, ProPublica, buybacks, retirement and housing outcomes, lobbying and tax expenditures); December raise vs premium; conclusion. Reproduce: FICA, withholding and refund, property-tax share, $39,886/$62,086 totals, SS cap 2.2%, 59% FICA rise. Errors: paycheck deductions inconsistent with net pay (Mike $637/$528/$463; Sarah $748 vs $621); the $48 monthly surplus is really a $952 deficit; the card balance is double the narrative; 2020 ITEP figures wrong; "75% of shareholders top 1%" wrong; the $2,000 child credit stale for 2025; the federal total uses the pre-credit tax; German benefits overstated. The stored ending is complete.
beat_map: Federal return, child tax credit, refund.
Structural shift: corporate vs payroll taxes.
International comparison: tax/GDP, health, child care, tuition, Germany.
Wealth concentration, CEO pay, ProPublica, buybacks.
Conclusion: composition not level; system rigged.
